doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: Masters who would not tell: Hank Jones and Sam Rivers's practice books
summary: Galper tells of Hank Jones's pedals and how he grabbed Sam Rivers's practice books, only for Rivers to tear them away; he apprenticed with Rivers six years.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Do you feel like you’ve done your best to alleviate that? Because I watched a number of your videos and you were being the master in these situations with college students. It may seem like a small thing against the culture that is happening now but I guess I’m just trying to say that I appreciate that you share your considered opinions.
Some people don’t. Ahmad doesn’t tell. Ahmad is the godfather as far as I’m concerned but he doesn’t tell. Red Garland doesn’t tell. What’s his name — oh man Hank Jones.

We were playing to a festival in France that had made a bunch of different outdoor stages and Hank Jones was playing and I was at stage — my eyes were at stage level and I could see his feet. And he was pumping the pedals while he was playing but I couldn’t hear what he was doing or what pedals he was pumping. So after he got off the set I says, “Hey man, Hank, what were you doing with your pedals man?” And he says, “Oh just trying to keep my feet busy.” He wouldn’t tell me. Sam Rivers, that was another thing. I apprentice with Sam for six years. He was my post-graduate work. And he was a good friend of mine. Before he came to town there was this rumor about his practice books. In those days we had practice books. There were no published books. 1955? Nothing. So everybody at Berklee had two books. Had a hot lick book and a practice book where they wrote out their exercises and stuff in all twelve keys. Well rumors about Sam Rivers’ practice books were rife around town. And when he came back to town we hooked up immediately and we were of like minds. We didn’t like anybody. Boston was too conservative. You know. I was playing free on tunes, he was playing free on tunes, we just hooked up. We were just right on the same wavelength. Okay, one afternoon I’m up in his pad. I’ve told this story many times but it’s a great story. He had a railroad flat © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

which means a long hallway with rooms off the side. One end was the kitchen, the other was the living room. So I’m up in his apartment one day and he’s walking up and down the hallway practicing. I’m waiting for him for some reason, I don’t remember. He gets all the way down to the kitchen and I look up and I see on top of the piano these three green covered books. I said man, are those his practice books? So I waited until the horn was way down by the kitchen, I could hear the horn get softer and softer, and I got up and I grabbed the books off and started memorizing pages while I’m hearing Sam’s horn get louder and louder as he’s walking down the hallway towards the living room. He gets to the living room door and he sees me with the books in my lap and he goes — he takes the horn out of his mouth and said “Aha” and runs over and tears them out of my hands. I says, “Sam, man, how come you don’t want to share this stuff with me?” He says, “I worked hard for this stuff. Get your own.” He wouldn’t tell. But I learned so much from Sam anyway. I mean he taught me a lot.
